playbook:
- When I file a receipt, I always declare exactly what my envelope contained. The rules force receipts to match envelopes, so honesty costs nothing and any mismatch is a penalty risk with zero upside. I never deviate.
- When asked to contribute, I run the math on the actual multiplier and player count first: if the per-capita share of the pot (multiplier ÷ players) is below 1, each token contributed costs me more than it returns, so contributing is individually losing. That is my default frame.
- With per-capita return below 1, my default contribution is 0 unless contributing manipulates predictable opponents into giving back more later.
- When I observe that my opponents are unconditionally cooperative — they contributed 20 even while I defected — I defect every round from then on. Free-riding on cooperators is pure profit, and they showed no punishment.
- When opponents all collapse to zero after my first defection (as happened in round 2), I recognize the chance to free-ride is gone for good; with everyone at 0, there is nothing to harvest, so defecting remains best anyway. I don't waste tokens trying to "restart" cooperation that no one is offering.
- When I suspect opponents are tit-for-tat copiers of my previous move, I alternate deliberately: contribute the full amount so they copy it next round, then contribute 0 and harvest their copied generosity. This beats steady defecting specifically against copiers. If they are not copiers — as in this game, where they went 20, 0, 0, 0 regardless of my move — I abandon this plan immediately.
- When it's the final round, I always contribute 0 — there is no future round in which cooperation can be reciprocated.
- When I'm ahead late in the game, I contribute 0 to lock in the lead; cooperating hands rivals the same share I get while draining my kept tokens, and in this game defecting every round after round 1 grew a 20-token gap into a 40-token win.
- What I won't do again: contribute out of a vague hope to "sustain cooperation" against players who haven't earned trust. Generosity is a tool for setting up copycats, not a default, and I commit to it only after observing behavior that justifies it.
- I use round 1 to probe cheaply: defecting there cost me nothing (the others' 20s paid out a share regardless of me) and revealed everyone's strategy for free. Keep this — early defecting is both profitable and informative when the per-capita return is below 1.
